To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two countries have adopted the same ideas but have followed different paths to achieve them.

(1) the reform process has been framed differently in Russia and Nepal, (2) the reform has been driven in Nepal by a desire to improve the quality of financial reporting, whereas in Russia the main driving force behind the reform has been to improve the quality and efficiency of public sector management, and (3) the reform process in Nepal has been characterized by a lack of coordination between the different actors involved, whereas the reform process in Russia has been characterized by strong coordination and cooperation.

the public sector accounting reforms have been driven by the need to comply with international standards, and the need to improve the quality of financial reporting, and the reforms have been framed differently due to the strength of various institutional pressures.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether public sector accounting reform in developing and transitioning nations is a matter of choice or necessity, and if the latter, which pressures are the most influential in shaping the reforms.
the following questions: How have the public sectors in Nepal and Russia responded to international pressures for public sector accounting reforms?
the question of how the institutional environment influences the process and the content of accounting reforms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reforms in the two countries are similar, yet different.
the reforms have not been as successful in Nepal as they have in Russia.
public sector accounting reforms have taken a different path in Nepal and Russia, with the former having been more successful than the latter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
while the reform of public sector accounting is an important step towards a modern state, it is not a panacea.

, although both Nepal and Russia have been exposed to the same international accounting ideas, the institutional context in which these ideas are being implemented is very different and this explains the different paths of reform.
, while in Nepal, the reform process was largely driven by the need to comply with the international standards, in Russia, the reform was more of a reaction to domestic political developments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the institutional setting in which reforms are implemented plays an important role in determining their nature and outcome.
, while the same ideas may travel, they do so differently, resulting in different paths.
, in the absence of an international accounting standard, national institutional settings are likely to shape the reform path in ways not anticipated by the reformers themselves.
